bio:
Born in Korea and raised in the United States from high school age, I spent nearly a decade immersed in American culture before returning to Korea to complete my military service. Afterward, I pursued my passion for design and art by studying Transportation Design at ArtCenter College of Design in Pasadena, California. I later returned to Korea to focus on both family and creative work, eventually transitioning into the arts full-time.

Today, I operate an art studio where I guide aspiring design students in building their portfolios, while continuing to develop my personal body of work. My artistic practice focuses on vibrant, emotionally driven acrylic paintings. My main series captures fruit splashing into water—each piece symbolizing a dream being realized. For me, the moment of impact between fruit and water is a metaphor for transformation, struggle, and hope.

The banana, for example, holds special meaning as a symbol of the Asian American experience—navigating identity, facing racial challenges, and ultimately pursuing dreams despite adversity.

In addition to the fruit series, I also paint Disney characters, colorful varieties of daisies, and automotive imagery—each genre reflecting a different facet of my personal narrative and visual exploration.

bio:
I am both a painter and a florist.

For me, flowers represent both inhalation and exhalation. While working with flowers—touching them, trimming them, hydrating them, and deciding which stems to keep and which to discard—my body draws in a deep breath of sensations. The temperature, scent, and texture of the petals, combined with the atmosphere of the day, a sense of anticipation, and the quiet warmth of everyday life, all enter me like a breath.

Just as an inhaled breath must naturally be released, painting these flowers feels inevitable to me. It is not merely an act of visual representation, but a tangible trace of breathing, where the senses of the entire body are absorbed into the canvas.

I am deeply drawn to the moments where flowers meet everyday objects. At the boundary where natural lines encounter artificial colors, and where softness touches firmness, new temperatures and textures emerge. When flowers and everyday objects come together, they renew one another’s way of existing.

bio:
Artist Yeji Lee 

Instagram : yegylee034


Hi guys 

I think human life is essentially like play.
As children, we unconsciously play to learn about the world, make connections, and discover ourselves.
More than just entertainment, play is an important way to express our inner fires and desires.
As adults, we often lose the meaning of play as we become more grounded in reality.
However, the freedom and creativity of play is still essential for exploring our inner dreams and desires.
In play, we experience failures and successes and discover new possibilities by trying different things.
This process allows us to listen to our inner voice and discover what we really want.
Our relationships with others also play an important role in play.
Games with friends and activities that involve cooperation and competition give us the opportunity to share and support each other's dreams.
These interactions can help us reach for bigger goals.
In the end, we realize that our lives are like a play in which we are working towards our dreams.
We all have different roles on our own stage, and it's a journey to find our true selves through theater.
In this journey, we learn how to fulfill our dreams and make our lives richer.
Therefore, we need to continue our journey towards our dreams through play, through the joys and sorrows we encounter along the way, 
The joys and sorrows, the failures and successes, are all important elements that make us grow.

bio:
Hello, my name is Darae Lee, an artist who paints the small moments of happiness found in everyday life.

For a long time, I lived at a fast pace, always chasing the next goal — art school entrance exams, university, employment. I believed that once I achieved each milestone, happiness would finally follow. I was so focused on moving forward that I rarely allowed myself to pause.

One day, while walking home after what I thought was another productive day, I suddenly noticed the strong scent of grass in the air. The leaves and flower petals swaying in the wind looked as if they were dancing, and it felt like nature was gently telling me, “This is happiness.” In that moment, I was reminded of my childhood, when I used to play freely with nature and insects, feeling joy for no particular reason at all. That realization made me aware of how many small but meaningful moments of happiness I had been overlooking.
A turtle appears in every one of my works. The turtle represents me — moving slowly but steadily forward, sometimes carrying emotional weight, yet continuing on its path. Traditionally, turtles symbolize longevity and good fortune. However, my interpretation of these meanings is slightly different. To me, longevity means a life where happy moments last for a long time, and good fortune comes naturally when we maintain positive thoughts and appreciate the small joys in our daily lives.

I intentionally use bright, luminous colors and soft light to create a sense of warmth and emotional comfort. I believe that colors carry energy, and through vibrant hues and glowing tones, I hope viewers can feel a sense of positivity, calmness, and gentle encouragement. 

Through my work, I hope viewers can take a moment to reflect on the small joys they may have forgotten in their own lives. Happiness is not far away or extraordinary — it is always near us, waiting to be noticed in the present moment.

bio:
My work seeks to contain life. By life, I mean both living and existence—yet for me, the Life is also the Truth, the single truth I believe in. My practice is centered on this truth, for the longing for it arises in every moment of being. Through this continual emergence, I rediscover the reason for existence. The greatest truth I know is ‘Love’. Repeated attempts—and inevitable failures—to lay down the self and genuinely embrace others have continually returned me to gratitude. My work continues as a record of this passage. The world may call it art, but for me, it is the revelation of truth through lived experience—the testimony of faith.

The foundation of my artistic inquiry lies in the ceaseless operations of the neural network. Over seventy trillion neurons absorb and store experience and sensation, releasing them beyond conscious governance. The process is unending—sometimes abrupt, even in sleep. Within this current, countless ‘characters’ emerge and disperse in constant flux. They form the essential resource of my work: an infinite internal dimension, too vast to be fully captured—beyond the reach of language.

When these elements coalesce, they surface as lines, colors, directions, velocities, and movements. At times, emotion intersects with fleeting landscapes; at others, sensory echoes crystallize into physical force, or the grandeur of nature condenses into a single gaze. Dormant entities awaken, manifesting as abstract images and gestures. Outwardly, what appears restrained and distilled in my visual outcome—though set against the overwhelming totality of my neural activity—is in fact the magnitude I confront: the whole of what I perceive. To bring this forward, my methodology extends across painting, sculpture, installation, performance, and audience participation.

Exhibition space plays a decisive role. Space is not a backdrop but the stage upon which meaning is shaped. The environment, the season, the architecture, the audience’s movement—even subtle details such as scent and sound—are woven into the work. I design space holistically so that the full arc of the visitor’s experience, from entry to departure, becomes inseparable from the work itself. Just as my practice originates from the spontaneous convergence of unbidden fragments, I hope the audience generates new and unexpected meanings through each encounter.

Ultimately, my endeavor in art testifies that truth alone constitutes the very foundation and fullness of life. Amid countless variables and unforeseen events, truth has remained constant—transforming despair and regret into unconditional joy and awe. Every moment of my life has been sustained by it, and so my work inevitably points toward it. The purpose of my practice is singular: to draw nearer to truth, to share the grace and miracle of walking along the Way, and to extend a quiet invitation for others to walk beside it.

bio:
I am usually making oil paintings and wall installations.
My main interest lies in re-composing the refracted memories of urban surroundings that lie dormant in the subconscious and then appear. To recall something is to re-compose it, and to know or speak of a past event is also possible through re-composition. Today, our thoughts are even more divided and fragmented. In my paintings and wall works, based on a digital way of thinking, I employ layering and collage re-composition, which are important techniques in digital image processing. These are effective methods of revealing refracted memories. For me, a wall installation is a space where painterliness, as well as what distinguishes it from a painting can be shown.  if painting appeals more to the internal sensibilities, wall installation is attractive because it allows one to approach that is filtered out by painting. Its transitory character produces more free and direct feelings and expressions, and enables one to focus on the pleasure afforded by the situation in which the work and the space become one.

bio:
The continuous theme of my paintings is megacities, the lives within them, and the traces they leave. Buildings, construction sites, and their byproducts are the main subjects of my works, often described in vivid, contradictory hues. Since last year, my work has been going through significant development, both in materials and concepts, experimenting with new ingredients such as pine pollen and Korean paper.

I start a piece by covering the canvas with oil, pine pollen, and/or charcoal, sometimes with Korean paper and sanguine. Different combinations bring out subtle surfaces carrying unsettling energy. Cityscapes with elaborate detail are usually painted on red or black oil-covered canvases, while more expressive sketches based on photography are carefully fixed on the canvases covered with charcoal or pine pollen.

I aim to invite audiences to contemplate city life, as many people today share a similar living environment in urban areas, especially in population-concentrated megacities. The main viewpoints of my works are the exteriors of buildings, construction remnants with deliberate details and colors, and photographic images of infrastructure painted in selected materials. With them, I try to expose the hidden struggles and alienation of urban dwellers, the decomposition of the cities, and the resilience rising underneath.

bio:
- Brilliant Darkness -
In the summer of 2019, the sunset I encountered in Bali, Indonesia became a profound source of inspiration. From that moment, I began capturing the essence of Brilliant Darkness in my sunflowers — a vision shaped by the striking contrast between light and shadow.

Here, darkness is not merely the absence of light. It carries a paradoxical meaning — holding the promise of light to come, symbolizing hope, warmth, and healing.

Through bold textures and dense layers of paint, combined with vivid, primary colors, I seek to convey the energy and heat of the red sun. The flow of colors moving from darkness to light, and light back into darkness, reflects the cycle of life itself. Within that cycle, each of us may discover our own meaning of light.

Amid the fading sun and the rising of new light, I hope these works offer a quiet comfort — flowers of hope blossoming in the heart of Brilliant Darkness.

I hope my art can gently touch the heart and deliver small but meaningful healing.

bio:
I continue to explore human existence through the concept of the “puzzle.” For me, humans are not complete beings, but rather incomplete fragments that are constantly being formed, carrying loneliness and desire. We are each a puzzle piece, yet we come to form a whole only through relationships with others.
I am interested in visualizing the tension between the inner self and the external world, and the space that emerges between them. Through restrained compositions centered on black, white, and gold, as well as material elements such as mother-of-pearl and the expansion of color, I seek to reveal the layered nature of emotion and the complexity of human existence.
Through works such as the Human Puzzle, Shadow Series, and Pinocchio Series, I explore inner longing, desire for others, self-awareness, and the irony of human existence in various ways.
I believe that human beings discover themselves through others while continuously questioning who they are. And I believe that this state of incompleteness itself is both the way we live and the very possibility of our existence.

bio:
DONGZADONGHWI is a multidisciplinary artist based in Seoul, South Korea.
His practice explores the emotional and psychological landscapes that emerge between everyday life and imagined ideals, between inner states and external realities. Drawing from childhood memories of freedom and the tension between personal desire and societal boundaries, DONGZADONGHWI creates visual expressions that are both intimate and universal.

Working across painting, moving image, and animation, the artist transforms emotional energy into layered, symbolic forms. A recurring motif in his work is the “Bird”—a character that embodies raw emotion, silent transformation, and empathetic connection. Through vivid acrylic textures and symbolic compositions, the Bird becomes a medium for healing and shared vulnerability.

His work carries a message of hope and emotional resonance. In a world full of complexity and turbulence, he offers a quiet invitation: to feel deeply, connect sincerely, and believe in the possibility of growth and healing through art.

bio:
Rosie Park is an artist who grew up in South Korea and continues her practice between New Zealand and South Korea.

Drawing inspiration from nature, art history, and everyday moments, she primarily creates paintings that explore the harmony and balance between natural and artificial elements. She delicately captures objects that feel both familiar and unique, examining diversity and harmony through multiple perspectives.
 
Through still life, she aims to convey the inherent individuality and beauty within each of us. Since 2022, she has actively presented her work in Seoul through various exhibitions and collaborations.

Her paintings, characterized by a sense of warmth as well as cultural exoticism and uniqueness, have been collected by art enthusiasts in South Korea, Japan, the United States, Belgium, Germany, Italy and New Zealand.

bio:
My work is a journey to discover and document scenes that offer warmth and solace within the tapestry of daily life.

Although we navigate our busy lives while carrying our own worries and anxieties, the warm moments that we unexpectedly encounter provide quiet comfort to a weary mind.

My work is inspired by children playing in dazzling sunlight, affectionate elderly couples, deep friendships with loved ones, and the profound tranquility offered by nature.

I recreate these moments by drawing on memories and imagined scenes, translating them onto the canvas. While the spaces depicted may not exist in reality, they resonate as a familiar landscape to everyone. I seek to capture the glimpses of warmth that I have encountered over time.

Through my paintings, I aim to imbue landscapes and subjects with pure, vibrant energy, unfolding them using a soft, serene color palette to convey a message of healing and peace.

bio:
An artistic farmer. 
Farming and listening to nature.
Nature is great and lovely.

bio: Yerin Kim is a visual artist based in Seoul, working primarily in oil painting. Her work explores emotional states through peeled surfaces and domestic textures. She has exhibited in Los Angeles, Paris, Toronto, and Montréal, and continues to develop her practice through international residencies and cultural exchange.

Shin Je Heon (b. South Korea) is a sculptor whose practice investigates the concept of the affective body—a body shaped by entangled emotions, inner imagery, and perceptual experience. His research explores the “inner eye” (siman) as a site where unconscious sensations, memory, and emotion are translated into form. Moving beyond anatomical representation, Shin constructs fragmented and interwoven bodily structures that embody psychological states and relational tensions.

​

His work emphasizes visual tactility, engaging the viewer not only through form but also through the suggestion of touch, weight, and material resistance. Through processes such as molding, layering, and distortion, he creates sculptural surfaces that register traces of action and emotional intensity. His recent works move toward greater abstraction and symbolic reduction, emphasizing curved, simplified masses that retain a sense of organic ambiguity. Through this process, the body becomes less a representation and more a condition: a vessel of accumulated sensations, suspended between visibility and invisibility, presence and dissolution.

bio:
Hello, I'm Jung Minhui, a painter.  
Sometimes, whenever the weight of life grows heavy, I retreat into the sanctuary of my imagination.
Within the countless imaginary worlds I’ve created, there exists another self of mine — my dog, Rich.
Rich sometimes sits with her eyes gently closed, as if dreaming, or enjoys a quiet nap.
She spends her time in serene solitude, wholly immersed in herself.
In reality, I adore the vibrant bloom of spring and the dazzling warmth of sunlight. Yet the words I use to define what I love hold no power before Rich — for Rich is simply happy, no matter the season or the day.
Under the gaze of others — their harsh judgments and the longing for all that I lacked — I once believed I possessed nothing.
Clutching an unfillable empty box, I struggled through the weary days, yesterday and today, with nothing but diligence and quiet perseverance.
All the while, I turned away from the many things I truly had.
Longing itself is not a fault — but within it, I lost my way.
And then I pictured Rich with her eyes closed, relaxed and unhurried — free from striving, free from the weight of what must be done.
The keys that appear in my paintings are devices meant to unlock my closed heart, while the unopened letters represent stimuli from a world I am reluctant to face.
While my self in reality seeks meaning in all things, Rich finds joy effortlessly, needing nothing extraordinary.
Rich knows well that joy is not granted by others — its mere existence is precious.
I find myself admiring that kind of being.

When moments arise in which life feels whole, I wonder — could I exist solely in reality, without Rich from my imagination?
With the passage of time, surely the weariness and hardship of life will erode and fade.
In those moments, all I can do is bring Rich onto the canvas, fill the world around her, and in doing so, reflect upon and heal myself.
With the hope that one day I might live a luminous present, untouched by the sorrow of unmet yesterdays or the fear of uncertain tomorrows,
I fill my canvas with fragments of imagined scenes — as if they might one day become real.

bio:
EUAN GRID has been working on, a monochromatic flat painting. The work unfolds in two main currents: Pop Art and Dansaekhwa (Monochrome Painting). 

Dansaekhwa is a meditative canvas that erases color and accumulates gestures, presenting a space of profound silence in an era of visual noise. 

Pop Art is a structural homage that reduces the idols of our time to minimal lines and planes, reassembling them within a modular order to elevate pop culture icons into the most rational and universal symbols.


Dansaekhwa: The Thickness of Silence, The Accumulation of Time The unification of materiality and spirit achieved through the infinite repetition of gestures

The single color present on the canvas is not intended to reproduce a specific emotion or subject. It is a record of time—a testament to his physical struggle and communion with matter upon the confined plane of the canvas. The infinitely repeated act of applying, pushing, scraping, and recoating paint is not mechanical labor, but the trajectory of breath. In this process, the paint transcends its role as a mere pigment; it becomes a breathing flesh with its own thickness. 

Euan views the canvas not as a mere substrate for depiction, but as a unified field where materiality and his physical actions melt into one. Modern individuals live in a world filled with visual noise. In this era of overwhelming ‘fullness,’ Euan aims to paradoxically offer the audience a space of perfect ‘emptiness.’ Standing before his Dansaekhwa—which appears empty yet is condensed with countless gestures—the viewer will break free from the obsession of interpreting images and viscerally sense the quiet vibrations emanating from the work. To pause one’s gaze and listen to the inner voice—this is the most powerful dialogue that this silent canvas initiates.

Pop Art: Reduced Signs, Icons Reconstructed through Modules A rational homage constructed by compressing and fragmenting the subject’s uniqueness into a minimal visual language

Euan’s Pop Art practice begins with an observation that reduces the signature poses of celebrities and iconic characters, deeply engraved in the public mind, into their most essential lines and planes. The process of boldly stripping away the complex narratives and unnecessary ornamentation of the subject, leaving only the minimal structural framework, is an act of transforming specific figures or cartoon characters into universal visual signs, devoid of emotion. Concise outlines and extremely restrained, flat colors erase the blind aura of the original, replacing the subject with a pure morphological symbol. These minimally simplified icons are then fragmented and reassembled on the canvas as independent, standardized modules. The seemingly solid myths and heroic poses of our time are broken down into countless units within a mathematical grid, losing their original context and acquiring a new geometric order. This goes beyond the mere appropriation of pop culture representations; it is the most rational and analytical form of homage, structurally dissecting and reconstructing the reality of the subjects we consume. The mechanically controlled, sleek surface and the flawlessly neat finish serve as a metaphor for the homogeneous screens of modern digital media, where content scrolls smoothly without friction. Within this refined canvas, viewers experience a visual labyrinth where familiar fragments of glory drift, deconstructed into a minimal arrangement of modules. Through this rationally controlled, minimal visual language, the work chillingly questions how the absolute subjects we so enthusiastically consume are ultimately nothing more than a combination of abstract signs.

bio:
I am a contemporary painter who questions the mechanical hierarchy controlling our modern visual environment, translating digital image fragments into the language of painting.

My practice of "re-focusing" on peripheral elements stems from a habit of magnifying casual snapshots to explore their hidden corners. I capture and crop the microscopic worlds that intrude as "noise" within high-resolution digital data. While these fragments are excluded as the "outside" by a camera's pre-programmed hierarchy, I amplify and anchor them onto the "inside" of a large canvas. This act is not mere mimicry, but a form of artistic act to escape the conditioned, non-human gaze.

The intense physical labor involved in this process represents my journey of wandering and lingering through uncertainty to re-discover innate human senses. Unlike machines programmed for absolute efficiency, we as humans often pause at the peripheral and embrace daily uncertainties. This "wandering" mirrors my process of exploring and filtering the overlooked remnants hidden within smoothly calibrated digital images.

bio:
Based in Seoul, South Korea, the artist brings a rich background in visual storytelling, having spent over a decade as a professional illustrator following her studies in Visual Design at Kookmin University. Her transition into fine arts was solidified by an MFA in Painting from Hongik University, marking the beginning of her dedicated exploration of the canvas. 
Her work explores the themes of psychological stability and healing, addressing the inherent anxieties of contemporary life through imagery of imagined gardens, animals, and nature. By employing a pointillist rhythm created with layers of gesso and acrylic, she generates a delicate vibration of color across the surface, transcending physical materiality to reveal a profound sensory dimension. 
These "gardens" are not mere escapes into fantasy but internal sanctuaries built upon a foundation of tranquility. Acting as a threshold where reality meets the ideal, her paintings serve as conduits for peace, inviting viewers into a meditative space of emotional rest and reflection.

bio:
I create scenes where emotions dwell—moments suspended between reality and something just beyond. Through a language of hyperrealism, I quietly portray the emotional topography of modern life, where things appear familiar yet subtly surreal. These are not depictions of fantasy as escape, but invitations to revisit the emotional truths we’ve set aside.

In a world where unfulfilled desires, misunderstood feelings, and unresolved emptiness often define our experience, we dream—not to escape, but to endure. My work seeks to materialize those dreams into visual form and gently return them to reality. I use precise realism to capture the surface of the world while introducing a sense of emotional dissonance through manipulated scale, softened light, and unexpected spatial relationships.

Recurring motifs include adolescent girls, companion animals, and fragments of ordinary urban life—street corners, crosswalks, playgrounds. The girl figure is not a character, but a mirror: suspended between adolescence and adulthood, she represents the incomplete self that modern individuals carry within. She stands for the vulnerable space between societal expectation and personal emotional maturity.

Beside her are animals—oversized, yet tender presences. Each one embodies an emotional need: dogs symbolize relationship and trust, ornamental fish suggest hope, and cats represent self-worth. Their exaggerated scale serves to visually articulate the weight and significance of those inner states. They are not just companions but emotional anchors—unspoken presences that offer comfort and reflection.

Light in my work is not merely illumination—it is an emotional medium. Drawing from digital visual language—lens flares, bokeh, halos, atmospheric blur—I retranslate it into paint to express the subtleties of memory and longing. The light connects disparate elements: the real and the surreal, the subject and the viewer, past and present.

The locations I paint are not fantastical. They are drawn from everyday life: familiar but recontextualized. In these recognizable spaces, subtle distortions invite viewers to project their own emotional narratives. The realism invites immersion, while the atmosphere suggests memory—blurry, tender, and open to interpretation.

I do not illustrate emotion; I suggest it. Through the tension of a hand, a sidelong glance, or a figure leaning into shadow, I try to evoke the feeling rather than explain it. My aim is to offer a still space for contemplation—a moment where a viewer may quietly reconnect with something within.

Ultimately, my paintings are landscapes of emotion. I try to dissolve the boundary between the seen and the felt, to create quiet rooms where memory, vulnerability, and inner life can re-emerge. These paintings are not statements but companions—silent presences that stay beside us, especially in the moments when we need them most.

bio:
I am a painter who reflects on how we see the world, how we remember it, and how we sense our own existence. Rather than focusing on accurately reproducing objects, my interest lies in the space between what is visible and what remains unseen—the subtle gap where perception and sensation gently waver.

Life is never entirely clear, and emotions and memories resist easy definition. I embrace this ambiguity and instability, believing that what cannot be fully grasped often reveals a deeper truth about both humanity and the world. Instead of offering definitive answers, my practice seeks to leave open questions, allowing reflection and contemplation to continue.

Figures appear in my paintings, but they are not fixed or fully determined. They emerge, overlap, and dissolve, existing in a state of becoming rather than certainty. These forms are not meant to explain objects, but to serve as vessels for memory, emotion, and traces of presence. Through form, I explore what lies beneath the visible—layers of time, lingering sensations, and the afterimages of the mind.

Through the use of light, negative space, layering, and blur, I suggest that the world is not a single, stable image, but a shifting sequence shaped by perspective and moment. Empty space is not absence, but a place where thought and feeling can dwell. Within this openness, viewers are invited to recall their own memories and experiences.

For me, painting is not an explanation, but a space for contemplation—not a finished conclusion, but an open-ended question. If a viewer can pause before my work and quietly reflect on their own emotions, gaze, and sense of being, that becomes the most meaningful outcome I hope for.

About Deconstructed Grid (Degrid)

While the formalistic grid of modernism (Piet Mondrian grid) had to remove all temporality, naturalness, emotion, literary illusion, and interactivity with the outside, Deconstructed grid implodes grid in meaning by re-expressing what the formalistic grid of modernism removed on canvas. The artist (Laila) expressed deconstructed grid through Goethe’s emotional colors, which she chose out of inner necessity.

Creative Artwork Process

My Deconstructed Grid works are more than paintings; they are sculptural objects born from a tactile dialogue with material. By blending stone powder with acrylics, I build a rugged foundation that is carved and layered to create a physical relief. Much like a traditional fresco, the mineral-based composition provides exceptional durability. These pieces are archival and resilient, standing firm against environmental factors such as humidity, UV light, and temperature shifts.

Techniques and Characteristics
Sculptural Painting: After layering mixed media materials such as stone powder and acrylic, the artist carves them back out through a labor-intensive process to complete a three-dimensional structure.
Durability: Using stone powder as the main material and hardening it through a pressing process, the work has a strong internal structure that withstands external conditions (temperature, humidity, etc.).
Lyrical Abstraction: Going beyond cold geometric structures, the works evoke the warm emotions of nature—such as spring flowers, spring rain, and snow—through visual expression.

Deconstructed Grid is an artistic concept presented by Western painter Laila Lee, and it is a series of works and an example theory that reinterprets the 'grid,' a symbol of 20th-century modernism, with her own philosophy.
The main features and meanings are as follows:
Artistic definition and philosophy
Overcoming Modernism: The formalism of modernism removes emotion, naturalness, and temporality from the screen, while "the deconstructed grid" restores it and imbues the artist's emotions into the grid.
Combination of physicality and spirituality: Attempts to combine matter (material) and spirituality by projecting psychological and emotional colors onto a flat lattice structure.
Communication with nature: Aiming for an open structure that communicates with the external world and nature by breaking down the artificial framework of the grid, and aims to capture 'nature before reduction.'

bio:
“I do not dream of the future. I embroider clumsy things upon aging ruins.”

Toyokawa is a visual artist who weaves the spiritual and physical decay, and the sense of lethargy that define South Korea in the 2020s, into a decadent tapestry.
Navigating the boundaries of graffiti, painting, and installation art, he dredges up the emotional dregs that society chooses to ignore.
In the cracks of an aging Korea, he expresses garbage, fragments, and the forgotten remnants of others.

His works are not assertions but laments — not eruptions, but submersions.
Disfigured memories, vaguely rendered subjects, and fluorescent colors chosen to simulate a forced sense of energy — these elements collide to metaphorically express the spirit of the age.
Toyokawa’s pieces evoke a subtle discomfort, and at times, are uncomfortably beautiful.

bio:
Shin believes that the longing for the original state of nature is deeply rooted in the human heart. In today’s world, nature is losing its original form amid threats such as  nuclear danger, climate change, artificial intelligence (AI), and biotechnology. We are becoming increasingly distant from the original beauty that humans so desperately desire. She thinks the Earth may be enduring the fear that one day all beauty may disappear. She wonders what untouched nature might have looked like in the  first place? And carefully place our crowns in the center of splendid and pristine nature. 

Shin believes that we are the crown created to shine above all else in beautiful nature. She believes that the crown, which has  traditionally been a symbol of authority and rule, symbolizes pride and self-esteem in an idealistic sense. As she reflects on her life’s journey, the crown she gives herself is not just an ornament decorated with gold and jewels. It symbolizes giving value to every moment of life, every challenge and the process of overcoming it. This crown gives her the strength to move forward, while the sparkling shards of light around her exist to protect and brighten our path. 

Morever, we who live in a modern society are always tired of the expectations that society demands. She believes that we should take the time to let go of everything and discover nature’s original form, so that even in our busy daily lives, we should not forget that each of us has our own crown, and remind us that we are inherently shining beings. 

Artist Shin has received numerous awards,  and had six solo exhibitions. She is active in domestic exhibitions and has participated in exhibitions in the United States, Taiwan, Monaco, Japan, France, Germany, and the Philippines.

bio:
Ming is a contemporary artist whose work centers on marimo as a living metaphor for continuity, quiet growth, and inner balance.

Rather than approaching marimo as a botanical subject, she treats it as a symbolic form—one that embodies time, repetition, and the rhythms of life.

Drawing from Eastern philosophy and contemporary abstraction, Ming creates layered, meditative compositions in which marimo functions as a visual anchor and contemplative presence.

Through subtle color transitions, repetition, and layered surfaces, her works form spaces of stillness rather than narrative imagery.

Her paintings are created for slow engagement, inviting viewers to pause, breathe, and reconnect with their inner rhythm.

Ming’s works are held in private collections and are created as contemplative pieces for living and personal spaces.

bio:
Born in 1999 | Lives and works in Seoul | Visual artist who explores the dynamics of psychological and physical balance by translating repetitive tactile movements into structural forms.
_
I focus on the movements and sensations used to endure moments of psychological and physical instability. When I falter due to the noise of daily life or offhand remarks, I engage in repetitive, minor habits to center myself. These acts—walking a fixed path within a cramped studio or obsessively kneading soft clay and objects—serve as both a support system to sustain my swaying self and a motor that generates invisible energy.

These microscopic movements are translated into the core techniques of my practice. Stroking the canvas, rubbing the damp surface of clay, or layering the trajectories of bodily movements onto translucent fabric is a performance intended to leave physical traces of fleeting motions and sensations. These recorded traces create a visual rhythm, eventually forming a cohesive flow and structure. Furthermore, this leads to an imagination of creating paths that hold accelerated energy through the overlapping of these trajectories. I long to capture the sense of tension and dynamism left by these repetitive movements as a visible scene or state. Giving substance to the movements of "holding on" is akin to translating invisible, unspecified sensations.

This flow extends beyond the two-dimensional plane into space. Here, my "standing paintings" exist in structures that lean against one another or stand precariously. Composed of thin fabric, paper, and wire structures, these fragile forms react sensitively to the slightest stimuli. Yet, even within that vibration, they maintain their place by finely adjusting their balance. As I witness these unstable entities, I question the diverse ways in which different beings sustain themselves amidst their own swaying.

bio:
Past, Present, And... (A Positive Energy of Love)

The painting work drawn on the canvas consist of innumerable lines meeting each other as well as the colors overlapped with each other. It may be a plane called 'knitted pattern'.
When seen from afar, it looks like a single color, but when you get closer, you will experience an optical illusion due to the various paints overlaid only to feel an impulse of touching it.
In this series of work processes, I would recall a happy memory, and then, the memory would be projected onto the present time only to heal me.
The image of the knitted pattern would be completed, while imitation and recomposition would be repeated from my own perspective. In this process, my philosophy that "knitting is a positive energy and love" is reflected on the work. I continue to research into it to help the audience viewing my works at the exhibition to expand their emotion.

Energy, it is the source of life for everything alive.
Owing to the energy, new life would be conceived, breathing in mutual relationship with other lives.
Although invisible to our eyes, everything alive and moving gets the energy from the Sun to regenerate itself, releasing it.
Though such a process, we feel that we are alive.

I see the origin of the energy as a positive and infinite love like mother's warm womb.
I wish that the audience facing my works and exchanging their emotion with each other would be reminded of mother's love through the media of thread and knitting and thus, would have an opportunity to think deeply about the energy of life and essence of love.

bio:
Shin Chung is a Seoul-based artist whose work explores not what images represent, but how they are perceived. Drawing inspiration from film, social media, popular culture, and everyday observations, Chung collects visual fragments and reinterprets them through geometric forms, custom-mixed colors, and simplified compositions.

Rather than reproducing reality, Chung reinterprets familiar images through a personal point of view. Faces and identities are often reduced to geometric structures, shifting attention away from recognition and toward perception itself. By balancing familiarity and ambiguity, the work invites viewers to bring their own memories and experiences into the image.

Through this process, Chung reflects on the ways images shape memory, desire, and cultural identity in an age of endless visual consumption, inviting viewers to discover their own narratives within each work.

In my recent practice, this exploration continues into the Orbit Series, where distance, relationship, and emotional balance become central forms of expression.

bio:
R.DAM is an artist who explores taste not as a fixed sensation, but as a sensory structure shaped by place, time, and human gesture. Their practice begins with eating, yet extends beyond flavor itself into texture, rhythm, atmosphere, and the emotions surrounding a shared table. Beyond food itself, the work focuses on the emotional responses embedded within the act of dining.

For R.DAM, food functions both as a vessel for traces of vanishing emotions and as a material that reflects artistry itself. Gustatory experiences are translated into visual compositions, where color, pressure, and movement become equivalents of aroma, mouthfeel, and aftertaste. Empty plates, abandoned cutlery, and the atmosphere left after a meal reveal intimacy, hospitality, and the vitality of being alive. Through this process, flavor is transformed into color and texture into memory, creating a connection between food and art.

Ultimately, the work invites viewers to perceive food from a new perspective and to reflect on the relationship between gastronomy and art. It also proposes an immersive platform in which dining unfolds as a profound sensory and emotional experience.

bio:
I work with photography to explore light, form, and spatial tension within quiet environments.
My practice moves between minimalist still life, landscape, and architectural subjects, with a focus on clarity, balance, and moments of stillness.

[Title: The Essence of Life is Suffering; The Essence of Humanity is Desire]
I believe that suffering is the fundamental essence of life, and that true happiness cannot be attained without embracing it. My work is a process of visualizing the various forms of pain that inevitably visit us as characters, reinterpreting them through the lens of wit and humor.

My persona, the character 'Vanzy,' was born from a period of intense anxiety and inferiority during my thirties, when I spent half a decade as an obscure ceramicist in a basement studio. Even in those pessimistic circumstances, I was consumed by a desire for success. It was through scribbling self-deprecating doodles about this ironic situation that I first encountered 'Vanzy.' As Vanzy began to garner significant attention, this series of experiences led me to transition from a ceramic artist to a painter.

At one point, I believed I had completely emerged from the dark tunnel through 'Vanzy.' However, the darkness invariably returned. Through this, I realized that suffering is not an obstacle to be overcome, but an entity to be embraced. Since then, I began to give concrete form to my vague anxieties by turning them into characters.

"The default setting of life is suffering, and the essence of humanity is desire."
"As long as desire remains, suffering is eternal."

'Vanzy,' whom I once believed to be my savior, was actually the incarnation of desire and, ultimately, the root of my pain. Thus, Vanzy remains my persona and an eternal riddle to solve. This creative universe is an existential attempt to face pain and redefine its meaning.

Starting with 'Vanzy,' I am expanding my own 'Map of Suffering' by creating characters from the fragments of desire—such as self-loathing, boredom, nihilism, and solitude. Ultimately, the ultimate goal of my work is a form of artistic discipline: objectifying the pain that overwhelms me and translating it into a language of play, thereby embracing suffering as a way to pursue happiness.

Hyojin Kim is a Tokyo-based sculptor whose practice centers on metal casting as a means of exploring tension, balance, and the physical limits of the human form. Moving fluidly between traditional craft and contemporary production, Kim dissolves the boundaries between hand-driven processes and industrial techniques to develop a distinct sculptural language.

Her work is composed of interconnected human units that accumulate into complex structures, evoking states of suspension, resistance, and equilibrium. These forms emerge through an intensive, iterative process in which repetition, gravity, and material behavior play a central role.

Working across a wide range of casting methods—from beeswax and pine resin modeling to ceramic shell, gypsum, and vacuum casting—Kim integrates multiple temporal and technical layers within a single body of work. By maintaining full control over each stage of production, she establishes a direct and evolving dialogue between material, process, and form.

Her practice continues to expand internationally, with a growing international presence, including exhibitions in Europe and the United States.

bio:
My mother has painted for thirty years 
— not for fame, not for a career, but because she simply couldn't stop.

She is not a fine arts graduate. 
She is a woman from Cheongju, Korea, who picked up a brush and never put it down. 

Over three decades, she has  filled canvas after canvas with flowers, landscapes, and abstract worlds — entering juried competitions, showing in galleries, and quietly building a body of work that most people have never seen.

Until now.

I am her daughter. I grew up watching her paint — early mornings, late nights, weekends, holidays. 

These paintings are not inventory. 
They are  thirty years of my mother's life, stacked in her studio.

I am sharing them with the world, 
because they deserve walls — not storage.

Each original work ships worldwide with a handwritten story card.

bio:
Zeyah Ren’s work begins with an attention to fleeting intervals in nature moments when light glides across water, when day turns imperceptibly into night, or when memory diffuses into landscape. These thresholds are brought into spaces of contemplation, articulated through a painterly language where reflection and reality quietly intersect.

Through an uncanny gaze, He seeks to perceive the subtle transformations that unfold within scenes we often overlook. By capturing riversides, forests, and skies, the work moves beyond the notion of landscape, toward realms where presence and absence, belonging and estrangement, converge.

Sun-Min LEE is a Korean gayageum player, photographer, and interdisciplinary artist whose practice explores the convergence of music and photography. Her work integrates sound, image, and time into a single artistic experience, expanding the boundaries of traditional media.
She began developing her artistic practice in Berlin in 2015 and has been based in Hamburg, Germany since 2021. Alongside her artistic work, she teaches at the Hamburg University of Music and Theatre, where she engages with contemporary approaches to traditional music and performance. Working as a multidisciplinary artist, she moves fluidly between performance, photography, and sound-based practices.

Since 2019, her photographic works have incorporated NFT-based sound elements that allow viewers to access improvised gayageum performances through smartphone interaction. This integration introduces a time-based auditory layer to the still image, transforming photography into a multisensory encounter.

In 2023, Lee Sunmin was recognized as a traditional music performer whose work bridges minimalism and neoclassical aesthetics. Her work was introduced and critically reviewed by the National Gugak Center in Korea, positioning her practice within contemporary discourse on traditional music and interdisciplinary art.

bio:
The Layered Traces of Space: Where Memories Intersect

I find a profound sense of liberation in being a stranger in an unfamiliar place. In travel, the weight of a memory is rarely determined by the duration of time spent in a space; instead, it is defined by the fleeting emotions and external fragments that linger long after we leave. Even when we share the same "here and now," our memories diverge, leaving behind invisible traces that are entirely unique.

My work is an exploration of these traces. I gather curiosities and lingering fragments of "space," using the perspective of my present self to imagine the memories of others. On the canvas, I fragment and layer colors to overlay new narratives onto memories that are gradually fading.

The juxtaposed colors on the screen each hold their own territory. At times they harmonize in perfect stillness, and at others, they clash and divide. This visual language serves as a metaphor for our collective existence: a tapestry of diverse individuals, each carrying distinct thoughts and experiences. Through this interplay of color and space, I invite the viewer to witness how these differences eventually find a way to coexist and blend into a singular, vibrant harmony.

bio:
Pia Jaeyoon Kim is a textile artist from South Korea based in Europe. Her practice centers on soft sculpture using wool and fibers to explore themes of contact, otherness, and the boundaries between self and non-self.

Drawing from her background in textile studies and teaching experience in fabric design and dyeing, she approaches material as both structure and language. Her works often take on organic, tentacular forms that evoke unfamiliar, speculative organisms, suggesting an alternative ecology shaped by touch and sensation.

Kim’s recent projects develop a continuous narrative world in which soft, fragile materials construct resilient and complex bodies. Through accumulation and entanglement, her sculptures embody a tension between comfort and unease, intimacy and intrusion.

She has participated in exhibitions across Europe and continues to expand her practice through research-based and experimental textile work.

bio:
Through my work, I strive to convey empathy and healing. The act of creation, along with the conversations sparked by my art, has allowed me to confront and release emotions once buried deep within. Over time, these experiences have enabled me to gradually break free from the mental torment that once felt like an inescapable hell during my childhood. It was then that I came to realize—art is not simply about crafting objects; it possesses the profound power to heal, to transform, and to inspire change.
​
This is why I believe my story is not mine alone. In the end, <my> story intertwines with <our> story. Through my work, I hope to bring forth the emotions that lie hidden within us all.

The trees that frequently appear in my work represent both myself and all of us. These trees have no roots.
​
As a child, I saw myself as a deeply rooted tree, unable to move. The thought of leaving a familiar place required immense courage, and at that time, I was a coward. I feared change and challenges, clinging stubbornly to stability.
​
One day, I embarked on a journey alone. That day, as the wind swept across my entire body, I felt a newfound sense of freedom. For the first time in my life, I felt as if I were truly breathing. It was then that I realized—I was not just a tree, but a tree that could fly like a bird. Rootless, yes, and swaying with even the slightest breeze, yet free to stand tall wherever I wished.
​
-
À travers mon travail, je cherche à transmettre l’empathie et la guérison. Créer, échanger avec les autres à travers mes œuvres, m’a permis d’exprimer et d’affronter des émotions profondément enfouies. Avec le temps, ces expériences m’ont aidée à m’éloigner naturellement de la souffrance mentale qui, dans mon enfance, me semblait un véritable enfer. C’est alors que j’ai compris que l’art ne se limite pas à la création d’objets : il a le pouvoir de transformer, de provoquer un changement.
​
C’est pourquoi je suis convaincue que mon histoire ne m’appartient pas seulement. En fin de compte, <mon> histoire s’entrelace avec <notre> histoire. À travers mon travail, j’espère faire émerger les émotions enfouies en chacun de nous.

Les arbres qui apparaissent souvent dans mon travail me représentent, ainsi que nous tous. Ces arbres n’ont pas de racines.
Enfant, je me voyais comme un arbre profondément enraciné, incapable de bouger. Partir quelque part me demandait un immense courage, et à ce moment-là, j’étais une lâche. J’avais peur du changement et des défis, préférant m’accrocher obstinément à la stabilité.
​
Un jour, j’ai entrepris un voyage seule. Ce jour-là, j’ai ressenti, à travers le vent caressant tout mon corps, une liberté inédite. Pour la première fois de ma vie, j’ai eu l’impression de respirer pleinement. C’est alors que j’ai compris : j’étais un arbre capable de voler comme un oiseau. Sans racines, certes, et fragile face à la moindre brise, mais aussi libre de me poser où bon me semble.

bio:
Through minimalist compositions and carefully controlled light, Kim abstracts architectural forms into quiet yet charged images. The repetition of geometric structures and glowing surfaces evokes both monumentality and fragility, revealing a tension between material excess and emotional emptiness. While her work reflects a critical awareness of modern civilization and its systems of value, it does not simply condemn them.

Instead, Kim seeks subtle moments of hope within the artificial cityscape. Light functions not only as a symbol of consumption and spectacle, but also as a fragile sign of human longing and possibility. Her paintings invite viewers to pause and reflect on the psychological and emotional conditions of contemporary life, suspended between desire, isolation, and quiet optimism.

bio:
Core Riddle

A Painter Who Reveals the Invisible Truth
Stories Beyond Art, Records from Parallel Universes

Inspired at the age of twenty by Kant’s words — “the starry sky above me and the moral law within me” — artist Core Riddle has long pursued a creative journey driven by wonder and inquiry.

Since his teenage years, he has explored science and philosophy, religion and mythology, art and human nature. From the observer effect in quantum physics and the theory of parallel universes to the Book of Changes in Eastern philosophy, his wide-ranging studies have become the foundation of his art.

Core Riddle’s paintings transcend the notion of mere “beautiful images.” They become maps of thought — visual records that seek to reveal the essence of both the universe and humanity.

bio:
Jun sung Back is a Korean artist who represents the original voice of contemporary art. He creates original visual experiences through colorful colors and bold compositions, and his works artistically embody human emotions and social issues that can be found in everyday life. His artistic journey has crossed the boundaries between the real world and imagination, and he has built his own unique world of work through various mediums and techniques.

One of his major works, the "Walking" series and the "lucky box" series, are his representative works, which impress viewers through their sensual harmony of colors and forms, offering a new perspective on everyday activities. 

The "Lucky Box" series is based on the joy and excitement that began with the children's comprehensive gift set that I received every holiday during my childhood. The anticipation filled with the box while wondering what was inside the wrapping paper at that time, and the happiness I felt when I opened the gift will never be forgotten over time.

Through this series, I wanted to remind you of the pure joy and hope of that childhood. Today, we forget many things in our daily lives, but I hope that my paintings will come to me like a gift and convey small and precious happiness. "Lucky Box" is more than just a work, it was born out of a desire to present the joy and warmth that can be felt in life.

Jun sung Back has showcased his works at several domestic and international art fairs and exhibitions, receiving great acclaim. His works have been recognized not only in Korea but also on the world stage, and he has been invited to several international art exhibitions and biennials, and has won numerous awards. In particular, he was selected as the cover artist of "The best of Watercolor" for the first time in East Asia on Splash 22 in the United States, which attracted attention. His works are housed in several major galleries and institutions, including the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Seoul City Hall, and the War Memorial of Korea, and are highly regarded among art enthusiasts. 

The artist seeks to communicate through art, and his works provide visitors with new visual experiences and opportunities for deep contemplation. He continues to create and push the boundaries of contemporary art, and he will continue to inspire many people in the future.

bio:
How are you~^^ I'm an oriental painter , creative artist and director. Since I was 17 years old  ,I have been painting from work activities for 30 years until now.
My favorite fashion,interior design,classic music.
Fashion, interior industry also worked on collaboration with me  while as a painter.
The theme of  my work is " recovery " and "healing" and I really would like to give hope and joy to a lot of heart people  from my artwork.
With the deep inspiration of oriental painting, I am creating my own unique and unique painting work that is oriental and Western by combining the beauty of the margins of oriental painting, the method of expressing all emotions with one brush, and the essence of objects with lines and dots. I draw and sketch at once, expressing the beauty of nature well with one brush, and expressing the meanings inherent in it vividly as if the objects were moving alive, moving them vividly, touching and healing them
And I want to give you joy.
In oriental painting, to express the vitality of flowers and trees, dots called "taepoints" are marked at the end of the painting. When expressing the breath of life, these dots were used to express the vitality of nature in wild flowers.
It represents the "totae" of oriental painting as the breath of life, and it works with "the value of what is seen for the invisible."
Through life like "Tae-jeom," it took natural materials and turned them into works of joy in life. There are also times when we can miss peace when we experience hard times in a city. At that time, I looked at the sky and clouds and meditated on everything that did not change, expressed it with the material of nature and expressed the garden of life.

bio:
Daedo Jun is an artist and researcher whose work explores human interiority, contemplative spirituality, and consciousness as lived experience.

Rather than explaining or defining the human condition, his practice seeks to create conditions in which one may quietly return to inner awareness. Grounded in theological reflection, contemplative practice, and philosophical inquiry, his approach emphasizes silence, attentiveness, and an inward reorientation of perception. His work invites stillness rather than argument, presence rather than explanation.

Alongside his artistic practice, Daedo Jun has published more than twenty research papers and scholarly essays across fields including AI studies, consciousness research, and spiritual philosophy. These works are archived in international research platforms such as OSF, PhilArchive, PhilPapers, Academia, and Zenodo, forming an ongoing dialogue between reflective inquiry and contemporary thought.

In parallel, he maintains a visual art practice that gives form to silence and inner light beyond language. His images do not demand interpretation; instead, they function as quiet surfaces through which viewers may encounter their own inner landscape. Abstraction and restraint are used not to obscure meaning, but to suspend it—allowing attention to settle before judgment or narrative takes hold.

His work consistently favors presence over explanation, stillness over persuasion, and depth over display. Through both writing and image, Daedo Jun continues a contemplative exploration of forms of expression that do not exhaust the human interior, but gently allow it to breathe.

bio: Working in a tiny space in Seoul, I focus on sculpture and two-dimensional painting. My work incorporates humorous elements, aiming to create striking visual experiences that are impossible to forget once seen.

I have always been drawn to patterns — the invisible structures that give shape to complex systems. But it was my first drone flight over Australia that revealed nature's own version of that logic.
What began as a personal escape became a revelation: the earth, seen from above, is a world unto itself. The geometric channels of Western Australia's pink salt lakes. The fractal coastlines where turquoise ocean dissolves into white sand. The ancient, overwhelming mass of Uluru at dusk. These are not simply landscapes — they are the hidden logic of the natural world, readable only from the sky.
I am drawn to the tension between the overwhelming scale of nature and the unexpected order it reveals from a distance. Shooting with both drone and mirrorless camera, I pursue images that exist somewhere between photography and fine art — moments where the earth itself becomes the canvas, and distance becomes a new kind of clarity.
I am working with media such as drawing, photography, video, and painting under the main theme of “The Right to Be Happy.”

I am an artist based in Seoul, South Korea. My practice explores the intrinsic value of human existence, translating quiet moments of introspection into visual form.

The recurring yellow bird in my work serves as both a companion and a symbolic presence—an unseen guide that protects, accompanies, and gently leads. It exists alongside the human figure, sharing in the rhythms of daily life and offering solace in moments of fatigue and vulnerability.

Through this visual language, I seek to create a space of warmth and quiet reassurance, where viewers may encounter a sense of comfort, resilience, and inner strength.

bio:
Yesang Lee is a South Korea-based artist who explores the connection between energy and consciousness. Her work is shaped by a diverse background in economics, music, and fashion design, which brings a structured yet rhythmic perspective to her art.

Currently, her practice is rooted in the symbols of Korean Minhwa—traditionally used to embody wishes for health and harmony. For Lee, however, these traditional forms are not a fixed style but a starting point. She uses Minhwa as a visual language to study the flow of inner consciousness, currently moving from these classical roots toward a more liberated, contemporary expression.

Specializing in contemporary reinterpretations of Korean Minhwa, Lee explores the essence of "reality-creation" through professional-grade oriental watercolors and natural calcite. Her work transcends traditional boundaries, capturing the invisible light of the self with sophisticated technique.

With a proven track record of three solo exhibitions and multiple national art awards, Yesang Lee offers collectors a profound visual dialogue between ancient heritage and modern consciousness.

bio:
ArtRound 1375 is a premier South Korean art and design studio specializing in 'Pagegraphy'—a unique structural genre that deconstructs photography into three-dimensional relief sculptures and bespoke artwall features. Led by art director Won Young, an MA graduate from Camberwell College of Arts in London, the studio layers thousands of hand-cut, original photographic fragments onto structural bases, permanently binding them through an intricate sewing machine "system stitching" technique.

Utilizing premium traditional Korean mulberry paper (Hanji) and archival pigment inks, ArtRound 1375 creates tactile surfaces with physical, shifting shadows that react dynamically to ambient light and viewer movement. Based in Yangpyeong, the studio focuses on high-end commercial projects, delivering sophisticated, site-specific installations tailored for luxury hotels, corporate lobbies, and premium public interiors worldwide.

bio:
Woojun Lee is an artist working with photography as his primary medium.

His practice begins with everyday life and gradually extends toward elements of the natural world. Rather than merely capturing landscapes, he collects fragments of nature to construct narratives about the environments that surround us. He is particularly interested in exploring what constitutes a "landscape" and how such components come together to shape our perception of it.

His work captures the interactive relationship between humans and nature, translating these interactions into visual landscapes. Currently, he is engaged in a body of work that explores the human being as a mediator between the microscopic and the macroscopic realms.

bio:

Exploring the primordial essence and silent power of life through a philosophy that celebrates imperfection: "Every line, even the uneven ones, has its own unique charm." The work focuses on stripping away the unnecessary to reveal the raw, organic vitality found in natural forms.

Seeking a tactile honesty, the process uniquely utilizes the reverse (uncoated) side of the canvas. This intentional choice highlights the coarse, natural texture of the fabric, bridging the gap between digital precision and the warmth of physical materials. Based in the dynamic landscape of Seoul, this practice is a continuous journey to capture the still yet powerful energy found in the most honest and 'uneven' lines of existence.

bio:
Born in Korea in 1960, Korean-Canadian abstract painter. I am so blessed  by God, in veiw of the fact that I could have started painting at the age of 40. 
In earlier life of 20s, I had worked for news paper agency for about 8 years. 
Since then, I had been weaving through the occupations like a copy writer, assistant director in  theater company.
Even when I was nearing 40 yrs, I did not realize that I am destined to be a painter.
Of course, I am not a genius like Gauguin, I knew, but I could not resist my fateful gravity towards being an artist.
"It never be too late", God seems to whisper to me.
Of course, I feared skepticism of my artistic dream, intellectual vanity.
However I pondered over the reason why the notion of a painter had come to my mind even belatedly.
That is new vision left behind to me, grace by God, I believed.
I entered into Alberta college of art, Canada, in 1998,
having majored in painting, then finished it in 2003.
I have been working on abstract painting for 15 years,
particularly centering on color field and Minimalism recently.  
I have a strong aspiration of resurrecting Minimalism again since 1960s. It might be reckless challenge,
but also I feel that this too is fate for me to pursue Minimalism now.
On the strength the this style in my works, I offer dialogue with the spiritual calmness and meditation.
Ultimately the fundamental and purest manifestation of my works idioms point to evoking the art of contemplation and the objects of inward-directed quietness in our troubling time.

bio:
Korean sculptor Yea Ji Park, working between South Korea and France, explores human relationships and communication through welded metal. For the artist, communication begins with the act of making itself. The process of welding—joining, building, and shaping metal—is already a way of reaching out and connecting.

Her sculptures use simple, abstract horse forms and lines that act like a visual language. These forms do not give fixed answers. Instead, they open a space where the viewer can feel connection, distance, or misunderstanding. The work invites the viewer to take part in this process of communication.

The material itself plays an important role. Steel carries weight, tension, and traces of heat. The marks of welding remain visible, showing how the work was made. These physical qualities help express emotion and relationship, making each sculpture feel like a living state rather than a closed object.

This approach is connected to the Korean word “mal,” which means both horse and speech. By working with this double meaning, Park connects form and language, using sculpture as a way to speak without words.
education:
At the age of 12, the artist decided to pursue studies in France after encountering an image of a horse in a French history book. This decision led to completing all formal education in France until the age of 22. The artist graduated from École Boulle with a Brevet de Technicien Supérieur (BTS) in Design d’Espace, receiving a Mention for a conceptual renovation project of the Longchamp Racecourse.

After returning to Korea, the artist began learning welding at a tuning car workshop and further developed both theoretical knowledge and practical skills through a government-funded training program. Since then, welding has evolved beyond a technical skill into the artist’s primary sculptural language, which continues to define the practice today.
exhibitions: Since 2017, Yea ji Park has presented more than ten solo exhibitions and over forty group shows in galleries, and art spaces across South Korea. Her work has also been featured in more than fifteen art fairs in Asia, including the Affordable Art Fair Singapore, Hong Kong, Harbor Art Fair in Hong Kong, Tianhe Art Museum in China, and in Seoul and Busan. In 2024, Park’s sculptures were shown in France at Maison d’art Laurence Pustetto in Libourne expanding her practice to a wider international audience.
events: From June 28 to August 9, 2026, Yea Ji Park will present a solo exhibition at the Yangpyeong Art Museum in Korea. The museum is a respected public institution known for its strong focus on contemporary art and its support of emerging and mid-career artists.

bio:

We use a unique technique of melting copper wires with an oxygen welding torch and shaping them as if we were shaping clay. This is a method that I learned entirely on my own, and many professors have praised it, saying it is ‘a fresh technique that I have never seen before.’”

bio:
Artist Statement
My work envisions landscapes of sanctuary. The Where Wishes Rest series embodies emotions of recollection, hope, and purification. I perceive earnest wishes (yeomwon) as latent energies—an elemental force that draws moments of healing closer. Through the language of painting, I explore this energy and depict the journey of a heart that rises again.

I coined the term Karmadise, combining Karma (the law of cause and effect) and Paradise (an ideal or peaceful state). Karmadise represents a path toward a harmonious inner state through positive karma and intentional healing. It is a spiritual refuge, guided by compassion (karuna), sympathetic joy (mudita), and equanimity (upekkha), reflecting the Buddhist pursuit of liberation from suffering. This process invites inner reflection, the restoration of emotional energy, and the deepening of the meaning behind one’s wishes.

Within my work, the yearning heart rests in a sanctuary of longing, drifts through waves of purification, and emerges toward light. The repetitive rhythms of flowing lines represent the subtle vibrations of hope arising from inner chaos. I call this space a Ritual Sanctuary—a sacred site that transcends expression and offers emotional liberation and vitality. Art becomes a visual alchemy, transforming wishes into shimmering symbolic landscapes.

My motifs often reference healing symbols: tangled threads act as psychic membranes sewn from childhood wounds, especially memories of my late father. These threads, like a silkworm’s cocoon, preserve memory and spiritual practice. Drawing from Didier Anzieu’s psychic envelope, I explore inner protection as a visual skin.

Canvas functions as both filter and relic—purifying negative energy through layered brushwork and luminescent pigments. With oil paint, neon pigments, and light-reactive materials, my work glows in darkness, revealing ideal dreamscapes such as Wishing Shelters, Guardian Trees, and Lucid Dreams.

To me, art is both light in isolation and life itself—a purified space for the anxious mind. I hope the viewer finds a breath of relief in the healing waves that drift through the mysterious depths of the psyche.

bio:
I began my artistic journey with watercolor and spent much of my school years drawing. Although there were periods in my life when I stepped away from creating, art had always remained quietly within me.


In my late fifties, I returned to painting after many years away, inspired by the vibrant colors and symbolic beauty of Minhwa, traditional Korean folk painting. What began as a quiet rediscovery at a small art studio near my home soon led to unexpected recognition, including a provincial-level awards. 

Through my work, I hope to share the lively colors, warmth, and spirit of Minhwa with a wider audience.

bio:
Rakeum Rhee’s work unfolds within a conceptual world she calls the Forest of Noon.
It refers to the moment of noon, when the sun reaches its highest point and shadows disappear—a condition in which all beings are placed under the same intensity of light. This forest is not a physical location, but a state where distinctions, hierarchies, and opposing structures lose their authority.

Within this world, creatures that once belonged to different orders—predators, insects, plants, and other forms of life—coexist within a single scene. They are not arranged according to power, scale, or biological hierarchy, nor do they enact narratives of conflict or dominance. Instead, they remain together in a state that is already complete. Nature, in Rhee’s work, is not an object to be observed, but a condition that includes both the artist and the viewer.

Alongside her figurative works, Rhee develops the abstract series GIL, which extends the same worldview into a more condensed visual language. Drawing from traditional symbols of good fortune, she transforms signs and characters into layered forms that are no longer meant to be read, but felt. Through repetition and structure, energy settles into the surface of the painting, creating a quiet sense of stability and presence.

bio:
I work with oil painting techniques rooted in Renaissance and Dutch Golden Age traditions, with particular focus on chiaroscuro and multi-layered glazing. My practice explores how light can emerge gradually from darkness, allowing form to reveal itself through time rather than immediacy.

After more than two decades of technical research and studio experimentation, my work represents a contemporary continuation of classical painting methods that are rarely practiced today. Floral still life serves as a primary subject, not as decoration, but as a means of contemplating stillness, time, and quiet presence.

bio:
JINIE is a Korean visual artist whose practice is grounded in color psychology and emotion-based abstraction. Her works explore the language of color through intuitive gestures, layering, and performative painting. She works as a voluntary emotional surrogate, translating unspoken emotions into visual form with intention and empathy.
She interprets the emotional depth of Korean Pansori into visual form, blending storytelling and color in a meditative performance of painting. Through this process, she seeks to connect with the viewer on a visceral level, offering moments of pause, empathy, and quiet healing.
education: She studied Western painting, where she also earned a master's degree in art education. She later earned a Ph.D. in Health Science, specializing in art therapy—an experience that deepened her understanding of the emotional and healing power of art.
